title: Basic Recursion
description: Core recursion, reducing a problem step-by-step, recursive return values, divide-and-conquer, and recursion with data structures.
identify: Problem size naturally reduces at each step towards a base case
Requires building up a result using return values of recursive calls
Solving a subproblem is strictly identical to the original problem but on smaller input
appearsIn: Mathematical functions like power or factorial
Basic structural operations on linked lists or stacks
explanation: Basic recursion relies on the call stack to manage state. The key components are the base case, which stops the recursion, and the recursive step, which breaks the problem down into smaller, similar subproblems. Understanding the flow of parameters downwards and the return values upwards is crucial.

title: Subsequences - Pick / No Pick
description: At every index, make a pick / don't-pick decision. Foundation for subsequences, subsets, target-sum recursion, and many DP problems.
identify: Generating all possible combinations where order of elements in the original sequence is maintained
Finding subsets that sum to a specific target
Constraint where elements can be included or excluded independently
appearsIn: Partitioning arrays into subsets with certain properties
explanation: The 'Pick / No Pick' pattern explores the binary choice space for each element in an array. By either including the current element or excluding it and moving to the next, we generate a complete search tree of size `O(2^N)`. This pattern naturally transitions into Dynamic Programming by adding memoization on `index` and any tracking variables like `sum`.

title: Combinations - Multiple Options
description: Use a loop to explore multiple choices at each recursion level, then backtrack. Focus on reuse, duplicate handling, constraints and building combinations.
identify: Need to generate combinations of a specific size or target sum
Elements can be reused multiple times or there are multiple branches from each state
Order does not matter (unlike permutations), usually solved by keeping a starting index
explanation: Unlike the binary 'Pick / No Pick', this pattern explores a variable number of branches at each step using a `for` loop. The `startIndex` parameter ensures we only pick elements moving forward, avoiding duplicate combinations that differ only in order. Backtracking (`pop_back()`) undoes the choice to try the next one in the loop.

title: Permutations
description: Use every element while changing its order. Covers used[], swapping, frequency counting and duplicate handling.
identify: Need to arrange elements in all possible orders
Constraint to use all given elements exactly once
appearsIn: Generating all arrangements of an array or string
explanation: Permutations involve rearranging elements. The swapping approach fixes an element at the current `index` and recursively permutes the rest of the array. The `for` loop considers all remaining elements as candidates for the current position. Alternatively, a boolean `used[]` array can track which elements are already in the current permutation.

title: Backtracking
description: Make a choice → check validity → recurse → undo the choice. Covers grid exploration and constraint-based backtracking.
identify: Need to find a valid configuration on a grid or board
Exploring a space where many paths are invalid and need to be abandoned early (pruning)
explanation: Backtracking is an algorithmic technique for solving problems recursively by trying to build a solution incrementally, one piece at a time, removing those solutions that fail to satisfy the constraints of the problem at any point of time. Pruning branches early using an `isValid` check is critical for performance.

title: Partition / DP
description: Recursively choose partition points or operations and explore the resulting possibilities. Useful for partition-based recursion and expression construction.
identify: Problem requires breaking a string or array into contiguous segments
Need to evaluate an expression by placing operators or parentheses
Cost or outcome depends on where the split is made
explanation: Partitioning problems involve choosing a split point `k` in an interval `[start, end]`. The problem is divided into two independent subproblems: the left part and the right part. The overall result is a combination of these subproblems. This pattern inherently has overlapping subproblems, making it a prime candidate for memoization or Dynamic Programming.
